subject: science
title: Cell Structure and Function
objective: Explain how major cell structures support life processes.

visual.title: Cell systems image
visual.caption: A labeled cell diagram that connects structures to jobs: information, energy, transport, and protection.

teachingSupport.summary: Cell structures are easier to remember when they are linked to jobs in a living system.
teachingSupport.description: Learners analyze a diagram, diagnose a cell failure, and defend which structure explains the evidence.

diagramCallouts.title: Information
diagramCallouts.body: The nucleus stores instructions that guide cell activity.

diagramCallouts.title: Energy
diagramCallouts.body: Mitochondria transfer energy that cells can use for work.

diagramCallouts.title: Boundary
diagramCallouts.body: The cell membrane controls movement into and out of the cell.

helperNotes: Sort organelles by job category before memorizing names.
Use claim-evidence-reasoning for every cell failure diagnosis.
Compare plant and animal cells by structure and function, not only appearance.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Memorizing organelle names without knowing the job.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Ask what would break in the cell if that structure stopped working.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Confusing cell wall and cell membrane.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Compare support/protection with controlled movement across a boundary.

teachingSupport.confusionPrompt: Write whether you are stuck on organelle names, jobs, evidence, or comparing plant and animal cells.

funTasks: Run a cell city simulation where each role must keep the cell alive for three rounds.
Build a claim-evidence-reasoning card for one organelle failure.
Design a before/after image showing how a plant cell differs from an animal cell.

groupHomework.title: Organelle emergency room
groupHomework.sharedOutcome: Diagnose a mystery cell failure and present the evidence trail.
groupHomework.parentRole: Ask the team to explain why their diagnosis fits the evidence.

reward: Unlock the Systems Biologist badge after the transfer case, not just the first quiz.

sections.warmup: Compare a cell to a city system and name three jobs that must happen.
sections.teach: Organelles perform specialized functions: the nucleus stores genetic instructions, mitochondria transfer energy, and membranes regulate movement.
sections.guidedPractice: Match organelles to evidence-based function statements.
sections.independentPractice: Analyze a cell diagram and explain what happens if one structure fails.
sections.activity: Build a labeled model with a claim-evidence-reasoning note.
sections.reteach: Sort organelles by job category: information, energy, transport, structure.
sections.challenge: Compare plant and animal cells using three structural differences.

quiz.prompt: Which structure controls what enters and leaves the cell?
quiz.explanation: The cell membrane regulates movement into and out of the cell.

quiz.prompt: Which organelle is most directly tied to energy transfer?
quiz.explanation: Mitochondria are the major site of cellular energy transfer.

studentFacing.mission: Diagnose a living system by matching cell structures to the jobs they perform.
studentFacing.whyItMatters: Biology becomes easier when names connect to jobs and evidence, not memorized labels.
studentFacing.bigIdea: Cell structures support life processes by handling information, energy, transport, boundaries, and building.
modelSteps: Sort each structure by job category.
Ask what would fail if that structure stopped working.
Use claim, evidence, and reasoning to defend the diagnosis.
studentFacing.example: If a cell cannot control what enters or leaves, the membrane is the strongest suspect.
studentFacing.nonExample: Knowing the word mitochondrion is not enough; you need to connect it to energy transfer evidence.
studentFacing.quickCheck: For each organelle, say the job and one sign that the job failed.
studentFacing.studentSummary: Cell parts are system tools; each structure matters because of the job it performs.
studentFacing.tutorHandoff: Tell the tutor if you are stuck on names, jobs, evidence, or plant-vs-animal comparisons.

learningObjective: Explain how major cell structures support life processes.
successCriteria: I can connect a cell structure to a life-process job.
I can use evidence from a diagram or case to diagnose a failed structure.
I can distinguish a plausible function claim from a memorized label.
I can transfer the structure-function model to plant, animal, or engineered-cell evidence.
essentialQuestion: How can structure-function evidence explain what a cell can and cannot do?

knowledge: Cell structures have specialized jobs that support information, energy, transport, boundaries, and construction.
A structure-function explanation is stronger when it connects a failure pattern to a specific job.
capability: Diagnose a cell-system failure from diagram and case evidence.
Construct and defend a structure-function explanation.
reasoning: Infer the most likely failed structure from what the cell can no longer do.
retention: Retrieve organelle jobs through mixed cases rather than isolated label recall.
transfer: Apply the structure-function model to a changed cell type or designed biological system.

phaseModules.title: Read the system
phaseModules.studentAction: List the life jobs a cell must perform and predict what evidence would reveal a failure.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Cell systems map organized by information, energy, boundary, and construction.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name a job before naming an organelle.

phaseModules.title: Connect structure to job
phaseModules.studentAction: Trace one organelle from its structure to its job and the evidence of that job.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Labeled cell diagram with job callouts.
phaseModules.successCheck: The explanation includes structure, job, and evidence.

phaseModules.title: Separate label from reason
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort statements into structure, function, evidence, or unsupported guess.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can identify what a claim still needs to prove.

phaseModules.title: Diagnose a case
phaseModules.studentAction: Use a case card and cell model to identify the most likely failed structure.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can cite at least two relevant clues.

phaseModules.title: Defend the diagnosis
phaseModules.studentAction: Write or speak a claim-evidence-reasoning explanation and compare an alternative diagnosis.
phaseModules.successCheck: My reasoning explains why the evidence fits better than the alternative.

phaseModules.title: Show biological understanding
phaseModules.studentAction: Analyze a new diagram and defend one structure-function conclusion independently.
phaseModules.successCheck: The proof uses evidence, not only vocabulary.

phaseModules.title: Mixed organelle retrieval
phaseModules.studentAction: After a delay, match jobs to structures in a mixed set and explain one match.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can retrieve the job when the order and context change.

phaseModules.title: Design a better cell
phaseModules.studentAction: Apply structure-function reasoning to a plant cell comparison or an engineered cell with a new job.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can predict a structural requirement and defend it.

phaseModules.title: Choose evidence support
phaseModules.studentAction: Decide whether the next step is a diagram sort, prerequisite repair, alternate model, or challenge case.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name the evidence gap that controls my next move.

proofTasks.prompt: Retrieve three organelle jobs after a delay.
Explain one structure-function relationship with evidence.
Diagnose a cell failure from a new case card.
Complete a mixed Memory Vault organelle review.
Predict a structural feature for an engineered cell and defend the prediction.

feedbackRules.result: The learner named a structure without explaining its function.
feedbackRules.hint: Ask what would stop working if the structure failed.

feedbackRules.result: The learner treated boundary support and controlled movement as the same job.
feedbackRules.hint: Compare protection and shape with selective movement across a boundary.
feedbackRules.action: Route to alternate boundary model and retry.

feedbackRules.result: The learner cited a clue without explaining why it supports the claim.
feedbackRules.hint: Add the because sentence between the evidence and the function.
feedbackRules.action: Route to CER frame before a new diagnosis.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner can name structures but cannot connect them to evidence.
reteachPaths.action: Sort organelles by job, model one structure-function chain, then retry a smaller case.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot read the diagram or identify evidence.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Repair diagram-reading and claim-evidence-reasoning skills before organelle diagnosis.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner independently diagnoses changed cases.
challengePaths.action: Compare plant and animal cells or design a structure for a novel biological function.

parentTeacherNotes: Keep the lesson evidence-driven. A vocabulary-perfect response without a defensible structure-function explanation should remain below transferable mastery.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a text-based description of every diagram and a keyboard-completable sort.
Do not rely on color alone for organelle categories.
Allow oral CER explanation or labeled drawing when writing mechanics are not the target.
safetyNotes: Keep biological examples classroom-safe and do not imply medical diagnosis from cell analogies.
